Queue::visit¶

Back to Queue API Reference

Signature¶

template <class F>
decltype(auto) visit(F&& f) const;

template <class F>
decltype(auto) visit(F&& f);

What It Does¶

Calls f with the held payload, typed as its real type, with no kind check or accessor call needed up front – visit is std::visit over the Queue’s internal variant. f is typically a generic lambda ([](const auto& payload) { ... }) that uses if constexpr to branch on the payload’s actual type, since f must be callable with all four payload types even if it only does something meaningful for one or two of them.

This is the method to reach for instead of checking kind() and calling the matching accessor by hand, when the logic genuinely differs per kind and a single generic function can express all four branches together.

Parameters¶

f (callable)

A callable invocable with const Series&, const Note&, const Timeline&, and const Duration& (or their non-const equivalents, for the non-const overload) – in practice almost always a generic lambda.

Returns¶

Whatever f returns for the branch that was actually taken, forwarded through decltype(auto).

Examples¶

Example 1. A generic lambda that returns a different string depending on whether the payload is a Series.

pluss::Queue q(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}));
const auto label = q.visit([](const auto& payload) -> std::string {
  using T = std::decay_t<decltype(payload)>;
  if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, pluss::Series>) {
    return "a series with " + std::to_string(payload.numel()) + " elements";
  } else {
    return "something else";
  }
});
std::cout << "visit result: " << label << '\n';

Output¶

visit result: a series with 3 elements

The lambda’s if constexpr branch means the else arm never actually calls .numel() on a Note, Timeline, or Duration – it is only compiled for the branches where it is well-formed, the same way any if constexpr over a generic lambda parameter works.

See Also¶

  • kind: the lower-level, non-generic way to branch on kind.

  • invoke: dispatch to the payload’s own named methods, rather than running arbitrary C++ against it.
